identity.title: Traffic Light Simulation
identity.tagline: Three LEDs, one state machine — a real traffic light's timing, on a breadboard.

goal: Recreate a standard traffic light's red → green → yellow → red cycle using three LEDs and a timed sequence in code — the first project where the code isn't just "blink one thing," it's actually managing a small sequence of states.
simpleSummary: Make three LEDs cycle red, green, and yellow like a real traffic light.
howItWorks: This project uses exactly the same electrical idea as LED Blink, just three times over — each LED gets its own current-limiting resistor and its own Arduino pin. The only genuinely new idea is in the code: a real traffic light isn't just "on/off," it's a sequence of states that always happen in the same order, each held for a different length of time (green stays lit far longer than yellow). Writing that as a series of digitalWrite() and delay() calls in a specific order is your first taste of a state machine — a program structure you'll use constantly once projects get more complex than a single LED.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
circuitDiagramCaption: Three identical LED+resistor branches (D10/D11/D12), all sharing a common ground rail back to Arduino GND.

wiringSteps.instruction: Place all three LEDs on the breadboard with their cathodes (short legs) sharing the same ground rail.
wiringSteps.detail: Keeping all three grounded to one shared rail (instead of three separate wires back to the Arduino) is exactly how you'd wire this on a real breadboard, and it cuts your wiring in half.

wiringSteps.instruction: Give each LED its own 220Ω resistor in series on its anode (long leg) side.
wiringSteps.detail: Each LED needs its own resistor — you can't share one resistor across all three, since that would let each LED's brightness affect the others unpredictably.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the red LED's resistor to Arduino D10, yellow's to D11, and green's to D12.
wiringSteps.detail: Any three digital pins work — these three are just conveniently adjacent on the board.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the shared ground rail to Arduino GND.
wiringSteps.detail: One ground connection is enough for all three LEDs since they already share a rail.

code.explanation: allOff() exists so each phase of the cycle starts from a clean slate — without it, forgetting to turn off the previous LED would leave two lit at once. The loop() function itself reads almost like a script: turn red on, wait, switch to green, wait, switch to yellow for a shorter warning period, then loop back to red.

expectedBehavior: The LEDs cycle continuously: red for 4 seconds, green for 4 seconds, yellow for 1.5 seconds, then back to red — matching the rhythm of a real traffic signal.

troubleshooting.fix: Check that specific LED's orientation and its resistor's connection — since each branch is wired independently, a mistake in one doesn't affect the other two, which makes it easy to isolate.

troubleshooting.issue: Two LEDs are lit at the same time.
troubleshooting.fix: Double check allOff() is being called at the start of every phase — if you're modifying the code and remove that call, the previous LED will stay lit.

extensions: Add a pedestrian "walk/don't walk" LED pair on a fourth and fifth pin, synced to the red phase.
Add a push button that, when pressed during the green phase, shortens it (like a pedestrian crossing request).
Control the three LEDs with a single WS2812B/NeoPixel instead of three separate LEDs and resistors (see the RGB Mood Light project).
Drive two intersections that must stay in sync (one is always red while the other is green).
